source.filename: 2018-Soft actuator with stiffness and shape modulation Using 3D-printed Conductive Polylactic Acid Material.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: Ogden hyperelastic model (N = 1, alpha_1 = 2.7172, mu_1 = 0.1581 MPa) for silicone rubber (Dragon Skin 30) assuming large deformation isotropic elasticity and incompressibility
Isotropic elasticity, isotropic thermal conductivity, and isotropic electrical resistivity for conductive polylactic acid (CPLA) in finite element modeling
Lumped parameter assumption of uniform spatial temperature distribution theta(t) within the rectangular CPLA sample for the heat transfer differential equation
Linear approximation between CPLA resistivity and temperature (R = 0.01086*theta - 0.06138) to enable analytical solution of the lumped thermal equation
Linear elastic behavior below the proportional limit for CPLA during tensile testing to extract Young's modulus
control_variables: Tensile loading rates (3 mm/min for CPLA specimens, 500 mm/min for silicone specimens)
Heating rates during thermal analysis (10°C/min for DSC, 3°C/min for TMA)
Actuator dimensions (140 mm length, 20 mm width, 2 mm wall thickness, 10 mm outer radius)
CPLA sheet dimensions (135 mm length, 16 mm width, 3 mm thickness)

3D printing parameters for CPLA (100% infill, 2 shells, 0.3 mm layer height, 230°C extruder temperature, 40°C bed temperature, 90 mm/s extruding speed, 150 mm/s travel speed, -45° raster orientation, 1.75 mm filament diameter, 0.4 mm nozzle diameter)
Constant pressure applied during grasping mode comparisons (20 psi) and active payload tests (22 psi)
dependent_variables: Young's modulus and stress-strain response of CPLA
Glass transition temperature and melting points of CPLA
Thermal expansion coefficient (CTE), thermal diffusivity, specific heat, and thermal conductivity of CPLA
Electrical resistance/resistivity and temperature evolution during Joule heating and passive cooling
Bending angles (theta_1, theta_2, theta_3) at the three actuator hinges
Steady-state temperature distribution across the actuator
Grasping functionality across different object shapes and holding payload capacity (maximum weight carried)

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Conductive polylactic acid (CPLA) displays a 98.6% reduction in Young's modulus from 1 GPa at room temperature (25°C) to 13.6 MPa at 80°C, and fully recovers its stiffness upon cooling back to room temperature.

Differential scanning calorimetry indicates that CPLA has a glass transition temperature of 55°C, where its Young's modulus decreases to 60% of its room-temperature value, and exhibits melting peaks at 124.4°C and 154°C.

A lumped-parameter dynamic heat transfer model with linearized temperature-dependent resistivity accurately predicts the Joule heating and passive cooling dynamics of CPLA, with passive cooling from the glass transition temperature to room temperature requiring approximately 120 s for a 10 mm x 10 mm x 2 mm sample.

Finite element simulation integrating an electrical system, steady-state thermal analysis, and an Ogden hyperelastic structural model predicts actuator bending angles with discrepancies generally under 2 degrees compared to experimental measurements (with errors of ~4 and ~7 degrees occurring only at 18 psi for Hinges 2 and 3).

Localized Joule heating of selected CPLA virtual hinges allows selective bending at targeted segments while unheated segments remain rigid, enabling reconfigurable bending shapes under pneumatic pressure.
A two-finger soft gripper employing CPLA-embedded actuators can execute distinct grasping postures (scooping, pinching, and parallel grabbing) to hold objects of varied geometry and compliance.
An actuator can lock its shape by cooling the CPLA hinges to room temperature while pressurized, successfully carrying a payload of up to 800 g passively without pressure or electrical power input.

experimental_setup: Differential Scanning Calorimetry (TA Instruments DSC Q2000) measuring phase transitions from 35°C to 185°C at 10°C/min
Tensile testing machine (United Testing Systems SFM-20) testing ASTM D-638 Type I CPLA specimens across 10 temperatures (25°C to 80°C) at 3 mm/min in batches of five
Tensile tester (Instron Universal Testing Machine 3345) stretching silicone (Dragon Skin 30) dumbbell specimens per ASTM D412-15a at 500 mm/min
Thermomechanical Analyzer (TA Instruments TMA Q400) measuring dimensional changes and CTE from room temperature to 80°C at 3°C/min
Flash analysis instrument (NETZSCH LFA 447 NanoFlash) measuring thermal diffusivity, specific heat, and thermal conductivity across three 3D-printed CPLA specimens

Electrical characterization bench comprising a Peltier thermoelectric generator (PELTIER CP081030-M), RTD sensor (TE Connectivity PTFM102T1G0), Arduino microcontroller (A000073), and voltage divider circuit up to 55°C
Joule heating and natural cooling setup utilizing a Kepco power amplifier (BOP 36-6D) supplying 50 mA current to CPLA specimens

Fabrication equipment: Formlabs Form 2 3D printer for resin molds, QIDI Technology QIDITECH I FDM printer for CPLA sheets, silver conductive wire glue for copper wire attachment, and silicone encapsulation bath

Pneumatic testing platform: Fluidic Control Board (Paradox Robotics) controlled via LabVIEW, aluminum mounting clamp, 12V DC power source, infrared thermometer gun, and digital image capture for bending angle determination

Grasping and holding setup: two-finger gripper manipulating objects (plastic container, plushy football, candy-filled cup) and single-finger holding metallic weights (50 g to 800 g in 50 g increments) in active and passive states
future_work: Developing closed-loop control of hinge stiffness through electrical voltage adjustment to achieve arbitrary desired shapes under fixed pressure
Integrating miniature temperature sensors at hinge locations or utilizing the strain-sensing capability of CPLA for feedback control
Investigating simultaneous joint control of both pneumatic pressure input and electrical inputs for wider shape modulation
Adopting active air or liquid cooling via embedded fluid channels for speed-critical applications
Investigating optimal activation of CPLA-enabled finger joints for handling different objects
independent_variables: Testing temperature for CPLA thermomechanical characterization (25°C to 80°C)
Applied electric current (e.g., 50 mA, 60 mA) and voltage (12 V) for Joule heating
Pneumatic pressure input supplied to the SPA (ranging from 4 psi to 24 psi)
Active hinge activation configuration (Hinge 1, Hinge 2, Hinge 3, or all hinges activated)
Payload weight applied during holding tests (50 g to 800 g)
Thickness of CPLA samples in cooling simulations (ranging from 0.5 mm to 3 mm)
limitations_inferred: Thermal fatigue, cyclic life, and interface delamination between the silicone matrix and CPLA over extensive thermal-pneumatic cycling were not characterized
Hysteresis between resistivity and temperature was neglected in favor of a linear approximation, which may introduce model inaccuracy during dynamic transient heating
Natural cooling requires around two minutes, severely restricting operational bandwidth and grasping cycle frequency unless active cooling systems are introduced
Continuous power is required during the shape modulation and transition phase, which may impact energy efficiency during rapid dynamic tasks
limitations_stated_by_authors: Thermal activation limits the approach to relatively low speed applications (1 Hz or lower)
Passive cooling speed is limited by natural heat dissipation to the ambient environment (taking ~120 s to cool from Tg to room temperature for the tested sample)
Bending angle discrepancies between simulation and experiments increased at higher pressures (~4° and ~7° errors at 18 psi for Hinges 2 and 3)
Experiments were conducted in open-loop without closed-loop feedback control of temperature, stiffness, or bending angles
Achieving the passive shape-locked state requires actively pressurizing the actuator and activating Joule heating before cooling and depressurizing
Object grasping demonstrations served only as a proof of concept without optimizing joint activation for different objects
main_results: CPLA undergoes a 98.6% drop in Young's modulus from 1 GPa at 25°C to 13.6 MPa at 80°C, fully recovering its original stiffness upon cooling
CPLA has a glass transition temperature of 55°C (where modulus is 60% of room-temperature value) and melting points at 124.4°C and 154°C
Thermal conductivity of 3D-printed CPLA was measured at approximately 0.36 W/(m*K) and CTE was 169 µm/(m*°C) below Tg and 420.16 µm/(m*°C) above Tg
ANSYS FEA multi-physics simulation accurately modeled steady-state thermal distribution and pneumatic bending angles across 4 to 18 psi (errors under 2° for most cases)
Localized heating at selected CPLA hinges enabled selective localized bending while unheated regions remained flat, modulating actuator shape
A two-finger soft gripper demonstrated multiple grasping modes (scooping, pinching, parallel grabbing) for varying object shapes
In a passive locked state (zero pressure, zero voltage after cooling), a single finger supported a maximum payload of 800 g without dropping or failure
modeling_methods: Lumped-parameter dynamic heat transfer differential equation for electrical Joule heating and passive cooling
Linear regression fitting of temperature-dependent electrical resistance of CPLA
Hyperelastic material constitutive modeling using the Ogden model (N = 1) fitted to uniaxial tensile test data of Dragon Skin 30 silicone via least squares
Multi-physics Finite Element Method (FEM) simulation in ANSYS Workbench coupling electrical conduction (Joule heating), steady-state thermal analysis, and non-linear static structural mechanics
performance_metrics: Modulus reduction percentage (98.6% drop from 1 GPa at 25°C to 13.6 MPa at 80°C)
Glass transition temperature (Tg = 55°C) and melting peaks (124.4°C and 154°C)
Coefficient of thermal expansion (169 µm/(m*°C) below Tg, 420.16 µm/(m*°C) above Tg)
Passive cooling duration (~120 s from Tg to room temperature for a 10 mm x 10 mm x 2 mm sample)
Bending angle prediction error (<2° for most pressure levels; ~4° and ~7° at 18 psi for Hinges 2 and 3)
Maximum pneumatic operating pressure tested (24 psi)
Maximum payload capacity held in active (22 psi, 12V) and passive (0 psi, 0V) locked states (800 g)
possible_gap_implications: The findings demonstrate that while CPLA provides an effective, low-cost means of achieving variable stiffness and passive shape holding, the reliance on passive thermal dissipation creates a speed bottleneck; addressing this through active cooling channels, closed-loop thermomechanical feedback, and dynamic electro-thermal-pneumatic co-design represents a critical gap for practical soft robotics adoption
paper.research_objective: To propose a compact, cost-effective stiffness-tuning mechanism based on 3D-printed conductive polylactic acid (CPLA) thermally activated via Joule heating, integrate it into a soft pneumatic actuator (SPA) to achieve stiffness and shape modulation, validate its performance through finite element modeling and experiments, and demonstrate shape holding and payload carrying in a soft robotic gripper without sustained power input.
paper.research_problem: Conventional stiffness-tuning mechanisms for soft robots (such as granular/layer jamming, mechanical constraints, and ER/MR fluids) often require bulky pneumatic or hydraulic infrastructure, valves, external heating elements, high voltages, or additional actuators, increasing system size and complexity; developing an integrated, compact, low-cost, electrically driven variable-stiffness mechanism capable of holding shape and carrying payload without continuous input remains a key challenge.
paper.robot_type: soft pneumatic actuator (SPA) / two-finger soft gripper
stiffness_mechanism: thermally induced thermoplastic phase transition of 3D-printed conductive polylactic acid (CPLA) via electrical Joule heating
paper.title: Soft Actuators with Stiffness and Shape Modulation Using 3D-Printed Conductive Polylactic Acid Material
